claim: The Caenorhabditis elegans Prop1-like homeobox gene unc-42 is expressed in 15 distinct sensory, inter- and motor neuron classes throughout the entire C. elegans nervous system.
source: We show here that the Caenorhabditis elegans Prop1-like homeobox gene unc-42 is expressed in 15 distinct sensory, inter- and motor neuron classes throughout the entire C. elegans nervous system.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the expression pattern of unc-42 based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: All 15 neuron classes expressing unc-42 are synaptically interconnected.
source: Strikingly, all 15 neuron classes expressing unc-42 are synaptically interconnected, prompting us to investigate whether unc-42 controls the functional properties of this circuit and perhaps also the assembly of these neurons into functional circuitry.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing synaptic connectivity among unc-42 expressing neurons, supported by connectome analysis and statistical testing.

claim: unc-42 defines the routes of communication between interconnected neurons by controlling the expression of neurotransmitter pathway genes, neurotransmitter receptors, neuropeptides, and neuropeptide receptors.
source: We found that unc-42 defines the routes of communication between these interconnected neurons by controlling the expression of neurotransmitter pathway genes, neurotransmitter receptors, neuropeptides, and neuropeptide receptors.
evidence: The manuscript presents extensive experimental data in Figures 3-6 showing effects of unc-42 mutations on expression of these molecular markers.

claim: Anatomical analysis of unc-42 mutant animals reveals defects in axon pathfinding and synaptic connectivity.
source: Anatomical analysis of unc-42 mutant animals reveals defects in axon pathfinding and synaptic connectivity, paralleled by expression defects of molecules involved in axon pathfinding, cell-cell recognition, and synaptic connectivity.
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy data (Figure 9) and confocal imaging data (Figure 8) showing anatomical defects in unc-42 mutants.

claim: unc-42 establishes functional circuitry by acting as a terminal selector of functionally connected neuron types.
source: We conclude that unc-42 establishes functional circuitry by acting as a terminal selector of functionally connected neuron types.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive analysis of unc-42 function in controlling multiple aspects of neuronal identity and connectivity.

claim: unc-42 was isolated in classic genetic screens for uncoordinated locomotion.
source: unc-42 mutant animals were also isolated in classic genetic screens for uncoordinated locomotion (Brenner, 1974), and the gene was subsequently found to code for a phylogenetically conserved homeobox gene, homologous to the vertebrate Prop1 homeobox gene (Baran et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: unc-42 codes for a phylogenetically conserved homeobox gene, homologous to the vertebrate Prop1 homeobox gene.
source: unc-42 mutant animals were also isolated in classic genetic screens for uncoordinated locomotion (Brenner, 1974), and the gene was subsequently found to code for a phylogenetically conserved homeobox gene, homologous to the vertebrate Prop1 homeobox gene (Baran et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baran et al., 1999.

claim: Vertebrate Prop1 has been mostly characterized for its function in pituitary development.
source: Vertebrate Prop1 has been mostly characterized for its function in pituitary development (Watkins-Chow and Camper, 1998), but the protein is also expressed in unidentified cells in the cerebral cortex, where its function has not yet been analyzed (Sjöstedt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on vertebrate Prop1.

claim: unc-42 controls the expression of GPCR-type sensory receptors in the ASH amphid sensory neuron.
source: Previous work has shown that unc-42 controls the expression of GPCR-type sensory receptors in the ASH amphid sensory neuron and glutamate-gated ion channels in command interneurons (Baran et al., 1999; Brockie et al., 2001; Wightman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: unc-42 controls the expression of glutamate-gated ion channels in command interneurons.
source: Previous work has shown that unc-42 controls the expression of GPCR-type sensory receptors in the ASH amphid sensory neuron and glutamate-gated ion channels in command interneurons (Baran et al., 1999; Brockie et al., 2001; Wightman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Command interneurons display axon pathfinding defects in unc-42 mutants.
source: Moreover, these command interneurons were also found to display axon pathfinding defects (Baran et al., 1999; Brockie et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: unc-42 is expressed in 40 neurons located in the head of the worm that fall into 15 anatomically distinct neuron classes in the adult nervous system.
source: Specifically, we found that in the adult nervous system unc-42 is strongly and consistently expressed in 40 neurons located in the head of the worm that fall into 15 anatomically distinct neuron classes (Figure 1B, C, Supplementary file 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1 using CRISPR-tagged reporters and NeuroPAL landmark strains.

claim: At the first larval stage, unc-42 expression is detected in the same set of neuron classes as observed in the adult, with the addition of very weak and inconsistent expression in AVJ and SIA that disappears by the adult stage.
source: At the first larval stage, expression is detected in the same set of neuron classes as observed in the adult, with the addition of very weak and inconsistent expression in AVJ and SIA that disappears by the adult stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the embryo, unc-42 expression is first observed in a few neuroblasts before the bean stage.
source: In the embryo, expression is first observed in a few neuroblasts before the bean stage.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of embryonic expression patterns.

claim: At the bean stage, when most neurons have terminally divided, unc-42 expression commences and reaches the full complement of unc-42(+) cells at the 1.5-fold stage.
source: At the bean stage, when most neurons have terminally divided, unc-42 expression commences and reaches the full complement of unc-42(+) cells at the 1.5-fold stage (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for quantification of levels).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No unc-42 expression is observed outside the nervous system.
source: No expression is observed outside the nervous system.
evidence: This is based on comprehensive expression analysis using multiple reporter constructs.

claim: UNC-42(+) neurons include sensory, inter-, and motor neurons and display distinct neurotransmitter identities (glutamatergic, cholinergic, or peptidergic).
source: UNC-42(+) neurons include sensory, inter-, and motor neurons and display distinct neurotransmitter identities (glutamatergic, cholinergic, or peptidergic) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of neurotransmitter markers in unc-42 expressing neurons.

claim: There is no obvious lineage relationship among the UNC-42(+) neurons.
source: Moreover, there is no obvious lineage relationship among the UNC-42(+) neurons (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the embryonic lineage shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All UNC-42(+) neurons project into the nerve ring neuropil.
source: Despite all UNC-42(+) neurons projecting into this neuropil (Figure 1E), UNC-42(+) axons are not exclusively part of one stratum (Brittin et al., 2021; Moyle et al., 2021; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on 3D rendering of neuronal processes shown in Figure 1E.

claim: UNC-42(+) axons are not exclusively part of one stratum in the nerve ring.
source: Despite all UNC-42(+) neurons projecting into this neuropil (Figure 1E), UNC-42(+) axons are not exclusively part of one stratum (Brittin et al., 2021; Moyle et al., 2021; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of nerve ring strata organization with citations to recent literature.

claim: unc-42-expressing neurons are more likely to be synaptically connected to each other than neuron pairs sampled at random from the whole connectome.
source: We found that unc-42-expressing neurons indeed are more likely to be synaptically connected to each other than neuron pairs sampled at random from the whole connectome (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of synaptic connectivity using the approach by Arnatkeviciūtė et al., 2018.

claim: Network differential gene expression (NDGE) analysis confirms the significant association of UNC-42 expression with synaptic linkage (p=5.78×10−5).
source: This analysis indeed confirms the significant association of UNC-42 expression with synaptic linkage (p=5.78×10−5) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on NDGE statistical analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A total of eight homeobox genes each show a significant enrichment in synaptically connected neurons, both by the NDGE analysis and the methodology by Arnatkeviciūtė et al., 2018.
source: This analysis shows that the expression of a total of eight homeobox genes each shows a significant enrichment in synaptically connected neurons, both by the NDGE analysis and the methodology by Arnatkeviciūtė et al., 2018 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on extended statistical analysis of homeobox gene expression patterns.

claim: The set of unc-42(+) neurons includes a single sensory neuron involved in nociceptive behavior.
source: The set of unc-42(+) neurons includes a single sensory neuron involved in nociceptive behavior (Kaplan and Horvitz, 1993) and downstream inter- and motor neurons that have been shown, mostly through microsurgical removal or genetic manipulations, to shape the locomotory response to aversive cues, including neurons involved in reversal behavior, omega turns, backward locomotion, restriction of head movement, pausing, and locomotory speed (Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Chalfie et al., 1985; Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2013; Ezcurra et al., 2011; Gray et al., 2005; Hamakawa et al., 2015; Hart et al., 1999; Hart et al., 1995; Hilliard et al., 2002; Hilliard et al., 2004; Kindt et al., 2007; Komuniecki et al., 2012; Sambongi et al., 1999; Shen et al., 2016; Walker et al., 2009; Yeon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous literature on the function of these neurons.

claim: Animals carrying the canonical allele of unc-42, e419 (a premature stop codon in the homeobox), display behavioral defects that match the defects observed after functional disruption of normally unc-42(+) neurons.
source: Using an automated WormTracker system (Yemini et al., 2013), we found that animals carrying the canonical allele of unc-42, e419 (a premature stop codon in the homeobox; Baran et al., 1999), display behavioral defects that match the defects observed after functional disruption of normally unc-42(+) neurons (Figure 2; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on WormTracker behavioral analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: unc-42 mutant animals are not completely immobile as there are many locomotory components that are unaffected in unc-42 mutants.
source: This match is not simply the result of unc-42 mutant animals being completely immobile since there are many locomotory components that are unaffected in unc-42 mutants (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on comprehensive behavioral analysis data.

claim: unc-42 is essential for unc-42(+) neurons to exert their proper function.
source: Together with the previously reported inability of unc-42 mutants to respond to aversive sensory cues (Baran et al., 1999), this analysis suggests that unc-42 is essential for unc-42(+) neurons to exert their proper function.
evidence: This is inferred from behavioral analysis and previous literature.

claim: Loss of unc-42 affects unc-17/VAChT expression and hence cholinergic identity in all but one of the normally unc-42(+) neurons.
source: We found that loss of unc-42 affects unc-17/VAChT expression and hence cholinergic identity in all but one of the normally unc-42(+) neurons (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The expression of the unc-17/VAChT fosmid reporter in RMF and RMH neurons is mildly affected in unc-42 and lim-4 single mutants, but enhanced in unc-42; lim-4 double mutants.
source: The expression of the unc-17/VAChT fosmid reporter in RMF and RMH neurons is mildly affected in unc-42 and lim-4 single mutants, but enhanced in unc-42; lim-4 double mutants.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating genetic interaction.

claim: Loss of unc-42 affects the expression of ionotropic glutamate receptors nmr-1, glr-1, glr-2, glr-4, and glr-5 in a cell type-specific manner.
source: We examined the receiving end of chemical synaptic neurotransmission by analyzing the expression of ionotropic glutamate (Glu) receptors, nmr-1, glr-1, glr-2, glr-4, and glr-5, and two ionotropic acetylcholine (Ach) receptors, acr-2 and acr-15, in the unc-42(+) circuit. The expression and unc-42 dependence of the ionotropic Glu receptors had been examined before (Baran et al., 1999; Brockie et al., 2001; Wightman et al., 2005). However, we found that some of these receptors are expressed in different set of unc-42(+) cells than previously reported likely explained by our usage of updated reagents that more precisely identify neuron classes. We found the expression of each of these genes to be affected in a cell type-specific manner in unc-42 mutants (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Loss of unc-42 affects the expression of cholinergic receptor systems, specifically the AChR subunits acr-2 and acr-15 in the RIV, RMD, SAA, and SMD neurons.
source: Moving from glutamatergic receptors to cholinergic receptors, we found that loss of unc-42 also affects the expression of cholinergic receptor systems, specifically the AChR subunits acr-2 and acr-15 in the RIV, RMD, SAA, and SMD neurons and expression of the AChR-like des-2 gene in the AVD neurons (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Loss of unc-42 affects expression of the AChR-like des-2 gene in the AVD neurons.
source: Moving from glutamatergic receptors to cholinergic receptors, we found that loss of unc-42 also affects the expression of cholinergic receptor systems, specifically the AChR subunits acr-2 and acr-15 in the RIV, RMD, SAA, and SMD neurons and expression of the AChR-like des-2 gene in the AVD neurons (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Loss of unc-42 affects expression of the tyramine-gated chloride channel, LGC-55, in the AVB, RMD, and SMD neurons.
source: Moreover, we found that expression of the tyramine-gated chloride channel, LGC-55, which makes the unc-42(+) circuit responsive to tyramine signaling from the RIM neurons (Donnelly et al., 2013), is affected in the AVB, RMD, and SMD neurons of unc-42 mutants (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The effect of unc-42 on neurotransmitter expression is often not fully expressive or fully penetrant, indicating that unc-42 is not the sole determinant of these neuronal identity features.
source: We note that the effect of unc-42 on neurotransmitter expression (presynaptic neurotransmitter synthesis/transport and/or postsynaptic neurotransmitter) is often not fully expressive or fully penetrant, indicating that unc-42 is not the sole determinant of these neuronal identity features.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative analysis of marker expression defects shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Three neuropeptides (flp-1, flp-32, nlp-15) and one neuropeptide receptor (npr-9) were previously found to be dependent on unc-42 in specific neuron types.
source: Previous work has already shown three neuropeptides (flp-1, flp-32, nlp-15) and one neuropeptide receptor (npr-9) to be dependent on unc-42 in specific neuron types (Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013; Wightman et al., 2005; Wood and Ferkey, 2019).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claim: The highly patterned expression of neuropeptides and neuropeptide receptors is severely affected in unc-42(e419) mutant animals.
source: We found that the highly patterned expression of these peptides and receptors is severely affected in unc-42(e419) mutant animals (Figure 6A–O).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The flp-7 and flp-12 neuropeptides activate the frpr-8 receptor.
source: For example, the flp-7 and flp-12 neuropeptides activate the frpr-8 receptor (I. Beets, pers. comm.) and the flp-18 neuropeptide binds to the npr-4 and npr-11 receptors (Cohen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on personal communication and citation to Cohen et al., 2009.

claim: The flp-18 neuropeptide binds to the npr-4 and npr-11 receptors.
source: For example, the flp-7 and flp-12 neuropeptides activate the frpr-8 receptor (I. Beets, pers. comm.) and the flp-18 neuropeptide binds to the npr-4 and npr-11 receptors (Cohen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on citation to Cohen et al., 2009.

claim: Animals lacking flp-18, nlp-15, npr-9, and npr-11 display decreased backwards motion (i.e., decreased reversals).
source: For example, animals lacking flp-18, nlp-15, npr-9, and npr-11 display decreased backwards motion (i.e., decreased reversals) (Bhardwaj et al., 2018; Campbell et al., 2016; Chalasani et al., 2010; Yemini et al., 2013), thereby phenocopying the unc-42 defects that we have described here (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: flp-18 and npr-11 are expressed in command interneurons that are responsible for backward locomotion.
source: Among these, flp-18 and npr-11 are expressed in command interneurons that are responsible for backward locomotion, and we found their expression to be unc-42 dependent in these neurons (Figure 6C, K).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: npr-11 is expressed in the AIB interneuron.
source: npr-11 is also expressed in the AIB interneuron, and, like AIB-ablated animals (Gray et al., 2005), animals lacking npr-11 also phenocopy unc-42 in that they conduct fewer omega turns.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and citation to Gray et al., 2005.

claim: Animals lacking npr-11 conduct fewer omega turns, phenocopying unc-42 mutants.
source: npr-11 is also expressed in the AIB interneuron, and, like AIB-ablated animals (Gray et al., 2005), animals lacking npr-11 also phenocopy unc-42 in that they conduct fewer omega turns.
evidence: This is based on behavioral analysis comparing npr-11 mutants to unc-42 mutants.

claim: flp-21 and ntr-2 mutant animals display decreased backward motion like unc-42 mutants.
source: We found that, like unc-42 mutants, flp-21 and ntr-2 mutant animals displayed decreased backward motion (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on WormTracker behavioral analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: flp-21 is regulated by unc-42 in the ASH neuron.
source: flp-21 is regulated by unc-42 in the ASH neuron (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013), the sole sensory neuron in the circuit responsible for backwards motion in response to noxious stimuli.
evidence: This is based on citation to Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013.

claim: unc-42 affects the expression of the orphan GPCR sra-11 in the AVB neurons.
source: Beyond neuropeptidergic communication, unc-42 may also affect signaling via other internal signaling systems. We infer this from the observation that unc-42 also affects the expression of the orphan GPCR sra-11 in the AVB neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: sra-11 is involved in an associative learning paradigm and responds to an as yet unknown, likely internal signal.
source: sra-11 is involved in an associative learning paradigm and responds to an as yet unknown, likely internal signal (Remy and Hobert, 2005).
evidence: This is based on citation to Remy and Hobert, 2005.

claim: ASH senses high osmolarity and this sensory paradigm is disrupted in unc-42 mutants.
source: Among other modalities, ASH senses high osmolarity (Kaplan and Horvitz, 1993) and this sensory paradigm is disrupted in unc-42 mutants (Baran et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claim: A putative osmosensor, osm-10, is expressed in ASH and osm-10 expression is disrupted in unc-42 mutants.
source: A putative osmosensor, osm-10, is expressed in ASH (Hart et al., 1999), and osm-10 expression is disrupted in unc-42 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 3; Wood and Ferkey, 2019).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3 and citation to Wood and Ferkey, 2019.

claim: ASH expresses many putative sensory receptors of the G-protein-coupled receptor family, likely involved in the chemorepulsive function of ASH.
source: ASH also expresses many putative sensory receptors of the G-protein-coupled receptor family, likely involved in the chemorepulsive function of ASH (Vidal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citation to Vidal et al., 2018.

claim: The expression of several GPCRs and downstream G-alpha proteins in ASH were previously found to require unc-42.
source: The expression of several of these GPCRs, as well as downstream G-alpha proteins, were previously found to require unc-42 (Baran et al., 1999; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013; Wood and Ferkey, 2019).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claim: unc-42 does not control expression of the pansensory cilia gene osm-6.
source: Like other transcriptional regulators that control the individuality of distinct sensory neuron types (Alqadah et al., 2015; Masoudi et al., 2018), we found that unc-42 does not control expression of the pansensory cilia gene osm-6 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: All normally unc-42-expressing neurons are generated in unc-42 null mutants.
source: We found that all normally unc-42-expressing neurons are generated in unc-42 null mutants, that they express the panneuronal reporter normally, and that they are positioned in a manner that is not quantitatively different from their relative position in wild type animals (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on NeuroPAL analysis shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neurons that normally express unc-42 express the panneuronal reporter normally in unc-42 null mutants.
source: We found that all normally unc-42-expressing neurons are generated in unc-42 null mutants, that they express the panneuronal reporter normally, and that they are positioned in a manner that is not quantitatively different from their relative position in wild type animals (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on NeuroPAL analysis shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neurons that normally express unc-42 are positioned in a manner that is not quantitatively different from their relative position in wild type animals in unc-42 null mutants.
source: We found that all normally unc-42-expressing neurons are generated in unc-42 null mutants, that they express the panneuronal reporter normally, and that they are positioned in a manner that is not quantitatively different from their relative position in wild type animals (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of soma positions shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some command interneurons display axon pathfinding defects along the ventral nerve cord in unc-42 mutants.
source: Previous analysis has described that some command interneurons display axon pathfinding defects along the ventral nerve cord in unc-42 mutants (Baran et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work.

claim: unc-42 is required for proper AVH axon extension along the ventral nerve cord.
source: Since the expression of both reporters is either not affected or only mildly affected in unc-42 mutants, they allowed us to visualize ASH and AVH process outgrowth, revealing that unc-42 is indeed required for proper axon extension of both neuron classes; unc-42 is required for proper AVH axon extension along the ventral nerve cord, and unc-42 is required for ASH axons to reach the dorsal midline (Figure 8B, C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: unc-42 is required for ASH axons to reach the dorsal midline.
source: Since the expression of both reporters is either not affected or only mildly affected in unc-42 mutants, they allowed us to visualize ASH and AVH process outgrowth, revealing that unc-42 is indeed required for proper axon extension of both neuron classes; unc-42 is required for proper AVH axon extension along the ventral nerve cord, and unc-42 is required for ASH axons to reach the dorsal midline (Figure 8B, C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Loss of unc-42 affects the proper axon extension to the dorsal midline of a subset of other sensory neurons that normally do not express unc-42 (OLL, AWA, AWB).
source: We also noted that loss of unc-42 affects the proper axon extension to the dorsal midline of a subset of other sensory neurons that normally do not express unc-42 (OLL, AWA, AWB) (Figure 8E, F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 8E and F.

claim: The ASI neurons are not affected in unc-42 mutants.
source: This apparent cell non-autonomous effect is selective; for example, the ASI neurons are not affected in unc-42 mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Previous work revealed axon outgrowth defects in unc-42 mutants in the HSN, PVQ, and PVP neurons, none of which normally express unc-42.
source: The apparent non-autonomy of unc-42 function is further exemplified in the ventral nerve cord, where previous work has revealed axon outgrowth defects in unc-42 mutants in the HSN, PVQ, and PVP neurons (Wightman et al., 1997), none of which normally express unc-42 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on citation to Wightman et al., 1997.

claim: unc-42 affects the expression of the secreted unc-6/Netrin axon guidance cue in command interneurons.
source: As we will show below, unc-42 affects the expression of the secreted unc-6/Netrin axon guidance cue in command interneurons, which may provide a straightforward explanation for the non-autonomous function of unc-42.
evidence: This is based on experimental data that will be shown later in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of unc-42 does not affect the overall relative arrangement of identified neuronal processes in the nerve ring.
source: We found that loss of unc-42 does not affect the overall relative arrangement of the 19 identified neuronal processes with the part of the nerve ring that we were able to analyze (Figure 9A, B).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: The processes that are adjacent to one another in wild type animals retain their adjacency in unc-42 mutants.
source: We quantified this arrangement through counting sections in which two identified neuron pairs are adjacent to one another and found that the processes that are adjacent to one another in wild type animals retain their adjacency in unc-42 mutants (Figure 9C, D).
evidence: This is based on quantitative electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Chemical synaptic connectivity is reduced in neurons that normally express unc-42 in the pre- and postsynaptic neurons in unc-42 mutants.
source: However, we found that chemical synaptic connectivity is reduced in neurons that normally express unc-42 in the pre- and postsynaptic neurons (Figure 9C, D).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: In the connection between SAAVL and AVAL, the wild type animal makes 22 synapses across 50 serial sections and the unc-42 mutant animal makes only 2 synapses across two serial sections.
source: The most striking example of an affected connection in which both neurons are unc-42(+) is between the interneurons SAAVL and AVAL. For this connection, the wild type animal makes 22 synapses across 50 serial sections and the unc-42 mutant animal makes only 2 synapses across two serial sections in spite of the normal adjacency of the two processes.
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy analysis.

claim: In the connection between the presynaptic unc-42(-) sensory neuron OLLR and the postsynaptic unc-42(+) motor neuron SMDVL, the wild type animal makes five synapses in a total of 11 sections, whereas the unc-42 mutant animal makes only one synapse across two sections.
source: For example, in the connection between the presynaptic unc-42(-) sensory neuron OLLR and the postsynaptic unc-42(+) motor neuron SMDVL, the wild type animal makes five synapses in a total of 11 sections, whereas the unc-42 mutant animal makes only one synapse across two sections.
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy analysis.

claim: The synaptic defects observed in unc-42 mutants cannot be explained by loss of adjacency alone.
source: The above-mentioned process adjacency data indicates that the synaptic defects that we observed cannot be explained by loss of adjacency alone.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing adjacency data with synaptic connectivity data.

claim: Electrical synaptic contacts are abundant among the unc-42(+) neurons.
source: Electrical synaptic contacts are abundant among the unc-42(+) neurons (Figure 1D; Cook et al., 2019; White et al., 1986) and are formed by members of the innexin gap junction proteins (Hall, 2017).
evidence: This is based on connectome data with citations to Cook et al., 2019 and White et al., 1986.

claim: Electrical synapses are formed by members of the innexin gap junction proteins.
source: Electrical synaptic contacts are abundant among the unc-42(+) neurons (Figure 1D; Cook et al., 2019; White et al., 1986) and are formed by members of the innexin gap junction proteins (Hall, 2017).
evidence: This is based on citation to Hall, 2017.

claim: In unc-42 mutant animals inx-18a and inx-19 expression is selectively downregulated in those neurons that normally express unc-42.
source: We found that in unc-42 mutant animals inx-18a and inx-19 expression is selectively downregulated in those neurons that normally express unc-42.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: inx-19 expression is affected in ASH sensory neuron, AVA, AVB, AVD, and AVE command interneurons, in the peptidergic AVK interneurons, and the RMD head motor neurons in unc-42 mutants.
source: Specifically, inx-19 expression is affected in ASH sensory neuron, AVA, AVB, AVD, and AVE command interneurons, in the peptidergic AVK interneurons, and the RMD head motor neurons (Figure 10B), while inx-18a expression is affected in the AVK interneurons, the AVA, AVB, and AVD command interneurons, and the RIV inter/motor neurons (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: inx-18a expression is affected in the AVK interneurons, the AVA, AVB, and AVD command interneurons, and the RIV inter/motor neurons in unc-42 mutants.
source: Specifically, inx-19 expression is affected in ASH sensory neuron, AVA, AVB, AVD, and AVE command interneurons, in the peptidergic AVK interneurons, and the RMD head motor neurons (Figure 10B), while inx-18a expression is affected in the AVK interneurons, the AVA, AVB, and AVD command interneurons, and the RIV inter/motor neurons (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Expression of the broadly expressed innexin unc-7 is affected in a number of neurons in unc-42 mutant animals.
source: Expression of the very broadly expressed innexin unc-7 is also affected in a number of neurons in unc-42 mutant animals (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: unc-42 affects inx-6 expression in the AIB neurons.
source: Lastly, in previous studies on the function and regulation of the innexin inx-6, we had already shown that unc-42 affects inx-6 expression in the AIB neurons (Bhattacharya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work.

claim: Several components of locomotory behavior were affected in inx-19 and unc-7 mutant animals in a manner that is similar to unc-42 mutant animals.
source: To test whether loss of innexins phenocopies the loss of unc-42, we tracked inx-18, inx-19, and unc-7 mutant animals and found that several components of locomotory behavior were affected in inx-19 and unc-7 mutant animals in a manner that is similar to unc-42 mutant animals (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on WormTracker behavioral analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The prominent loss of expression of innexins is a strong indication that electrical synaptic connectivity is not properly established in unc-42 mutants.
source: Taken together, the prominent loss of expression of innexins is a strong indication that electrical synaptic connectivity is not properly established in unc-42 mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of innexin expression and behavioral phenotypes.

claim: UNC-6/Netrin is known to affect both axon pathfinding and synapse formation in C. elegans and other systems.
source: The most obvious candidate is the UNC-6/Netrin protein, which is known to affect both axon pathfinding and synapse formation in C. elegans and other systems (Colón-Ramos et al., 2007; Hedgecock et al., 1990).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous literature.

claim: UNC-6 is expressed in a highly restricted manner during C. elegans development, and the few sites of neuronal expression include the command interneurons.
source: UNC-6 is expressed in a highly restricted manner during C. elegans development, and the few sites of neuronal expression include the command interneurons (Wadsworth et al., 1996; Weinberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claim: unc-6/Netrin null mutants show defects in amphid sensory neuron axon outgrowth that mimic the effects observed in unc-42 mutants.
source: We found that unc-6/Netrin null mutants show defects in amphid sensory neuron axon outgrowth that mimic the effects observed in unc-42 mutants.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations comparing unc-6 and unc-42 mutants.

claim: The ASH axons display a 40% penetrant axon extension defect in unc-6(ev400) null mutants.
source: For example, the ASH axons display a 40% penetrant axon extension defect in unc-6(ev400) null mutants (n = 91), comparable to what is observed in unc-42 mutants (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of axon extension defects.

claim: In unc-42 mutants unc-6/Netrin expression is eliminated from all command interneurons.
source: We found that in unc-42 mutants unc-6/Netrin expression (as assessed with an unc-6 fosmid-based reporter reagent) (Weinberg et al., 2018) is eliminated from all command interneurons (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: The synaptically connected unc-42(+) neurons express a host of cell surface molecules with potential roles in axon pathfinding and synapse formation.
source: The synaptically connected unc-42(+) neurons also express a host of cell surface molecules with potential roles in axon pathfinding and synapse formation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cell surface molecule expression patterns.

claim: Expression of each of ten examined cell surface proteins is profoundly affected in unc-42 mutant animals.
source: We examined 10 cell surface proteins (nine of them of the IgSF family members) that show expression in subsets of unc-42(+) neurons for their dependence on unc-42. These include genes previously shown to be involved in axon pathfinding and/or axon fasciculation (lad-2/L1CAM, rig-6/Contactin, ncam-1/NCAM) and/or organizing synaptic structure and/or function (nlg-1/Neuroligin, syg-1/KirreL, rig-5/IgLON, oig-1, rig-3) (Hashimoto et al., 2009; Howell et al., 2015; Kim and Emmons, 2017; Maro et al., 2015; Schwarz et al., 2009; Shen and Bargmann, 2003; Wang et al., 2008), as well as two IgCAMs with presently unknown functions (rig-1 and rig-5). These proteins display a unique combinatorial expression in each unc-42(+) neurons (with the exception of AVK and AVH). We found that expression of each one of these 10 genes is profoundly affected in unc-42 mutant animals (Figure 11B–J), summarized in Figure 11K.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 11.

claim: nlg-1/Neuroligin and three IgSF members, rig-6/Contactin, ncam-1/NCAM and rig-3 phenocopy subsets of the unc-42 locomotory defects.
source: We found that nlg-1/Neuroligin and three IgSF members, rig-6/Contactin, ncam-1/NCAM and rig-3 phenocopy subsets of the unc-42 locomotory defects (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on WormTracker behavioral analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: rig-6 and ncam-1 mutants display fewer omega turns and are expressed, in an unc-42-dependent manner, in omega turn controlling neurons (ASH, RIV, or AIB).
source: Similar to unc-42 mutants, rig-6 and ncam-1 mutants display fewer omega turns and are expressed, in an unc-42-dependent manner, in omega turn controlling neurons (ASH, RIV, or AIB).
evidence: This is based on behavioral analysis and expression pattern analysis.

claim: ncam-1(-) animals phenocopy unc-42(-) animals in regard to increased pausing, a behavior that is controlled by the AIB neuron.
source: ncam-1(-) animals also phenocopy unc-42(-) animals in regard to increased pausing, a behavior that is controlled by the AIB neuron, where the expression of ncam-1 is unc-42 dependent.
evidence: This is based on behavioral analysis and expression pattern analysis.

claim: nlg-1 mutants phenocopy unc-42 mutants in decreased backwards motion, a behavior that is controlled by the AVA command interneuron.
source: nlg-1 mutants phenocopy unc-42 mutants in decreased backwards motion, a behavior that is controlled by the AVA command interneuron, where the expression of nlg-1 is unc-42-dependent (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral analysis and expression pattern analysis.

claim: Functionally validated UNC-42 binding sites are enriched in the cellular transcriptomes of each one of the 15 neuron classes that express UNC-42.
source: Using the single cell transcriptome atlas of all C. elegans neurons (Taylor et al., 2021) and a phylogenetic footprinting pipeline, described in the accompanying paper by Glenwinkel et al., we found that functionally validated UNC-42 binding sites are enriched in the cellular transcriptomes of each one of the 15 neuron classes that express UNC-42 including those genes whose expression we have shown here to be unc-42-dependent (representative examples are shown in Figure 12A) (Glenwinkel et al., accompanying paper).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of binding sites shown in Figure 12A.

claim: UNC-42 directly activates the expression of terminal gene batteries in all unc-42(+) neurons.
source: This analysis strongly suggests that UNC-42 directly activates the expression of terminal gene batteries in all unc-42(+) neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of UNC-42 binding sites in target genes.

claim: UNC-42 requires neuron-type-specific cofactors to activate distinct sets of neuron class-specific gene batteries.
source: The most parsimonious explanation is that UNC-42 requires neuron-type-specific cofactors to activate distinct sets of neuron class-specific gene batteries. We found this scenario to indeed apply in many UNC-42(+) neuron classes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UNC-42 binding sites are present in genes not expressed in all UNC-42(+) neurons.

claim: unc-3 affects the cholinergic identity of command interneurons in a manner similar to the unc-42 effect.
source: For example, we had previously shown that the EBF/Collier ortholog unc-3 affects the cholinergic identity of command interneurons in a manner similar to the unc-42 effect (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work.

claim: UNC-42 binding sites are co-enriched with UNC-3 sites in genes expressed in all command interneurons.
source: Consistent with UNC-3 and UNC-42 working together, we found that UNC-42 binding sites are co-enriched with UNC-3 sites in genes expressed in all command interneurons (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of binding sites shown in Figure 12B.

claim: In unc-42; unc-3 double mutant animals, defects in unc-17/VAChT expression are synergistic relative to the single null mutants in some of the affected neurons.
source: Building unc-42; unc-3 double mutant animals, we found that in some of the affected neurons the defects are synergistic relative to the single null mutants, indicating that both genes cooperate to control cholinergic neurotransmitter identity in the command interneurons (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3 demonstrating genetic interaction.

claim: Loss of the ARID-type cfi-1 transcription factor causes differentiation defects in the AVD neurons resembling those observed in unc-42 mutants.
source: Loss of the ARID-type cfi-1 transcription factor causes differentiation defects in one of the command neurons, the AVD neurons (Shaham and Bargmann, 2002) resembling those observed in unc-42 mutants.
evidence: This is based on citation to Shaham and Bargmann, 2002.

claim: The nuclear receptor fax-1 controls the expression of genes in AVA and AVE, but not AVD.
source: In contrast, the nuclear receptor fax-1 controls the expression of genes in AVA and AVE, but not AVD (Wightman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on citation to Wightman et al., 2005.

claim: The AVD gene battery contains an enrichment for CFI-1 binding sites (in addition to the UNC-42 and UNC-3 binding site enrichment).
source: We found that the AVD gene battery contains an enrichment for CFI-1 binding sites (in addition to the UNC-42 and UNC-3 binding site enrichment), while the other command interneurons display enrichments of FAX-1 binding sites (in addition to the UNC-42 and UNC-3 binding site enrichment) (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of binding sites shown in Figure 12B.

claim: The other command interneurons display enrichments of FAX-1 binding sites (in addition to the UNC-42 and UNC-3 binding site enrichment).
source: We found that the AVD gene battery contains an enrichment for CFI-1 binding sites (in addition to the UNC-42 and UNC-3 binding site enrichment), while the other command interneurons display enrichments of FAX-1 binding sites (in addition to the UNC-42 and UNC-3 binding site enrichment) (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of binding sites shown in Figure 12B.

claim: The AVK interneurons that require both fax-1 and unc-42 for their proper differentiation also display a co-enrichment for FAX-1 and UNC-42 binding sites.
source: Notably, the AVK interneurons that require both fax-1 and unc-42 for their proper differentiation (Wightman et al., 2005) also display a co-enrichment for FAX-1 and UNC-42 binding sites.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of binding sites and citation to Wightman et al., 2005.

claim: UNC-42 cooperates with UNC-3 and CFI-1 to specify AVD identity.
source: Hence, we surmise that UNC-42 cooperates with UNC-3 and CFI-1 to specify AVD identity and with UNC-3 and FAX-1 to specify AVA and AVE identity, and with FAX-1, but not UNC-3, to specify AVK identity.
evidence: This is inferred from binding site enrichment analysis and genetic interaction data.

claim: UNC-42 cooperates with UNC-3 and FAX-1 to specify AVA and AVE identity.
source: Hence, we surmise that UNC-42 cooperates with UNC-3 and CFI-1 to specify AVD identity and with UNC-3 and FAX-1 to specify AVA and AVE identity, and with FAX-1, but not UNC-3, to specify AVK identity.
evidence: This is inferred from binding site enrichment analysis and genetic interaction data.

claim: UNC-42 cooperates with FAX-1, but not UNC-3, to specify AVK identity.
source: Hence, we surmise that UNC-42 cooperates with UNC-3 and CFI-1 to specify AVD identity and with UNC-3 and FAX-1 to specify AVA and AVE identity, and with FAX-1, but not UNC-3, to specify AVK identity.
evidence: This is inferred from binding site enrichment analysis and genetic interaction data.

claim: unc-42 single mutants have mild defects in execution of cholinergic fate of RMF and RMH neurons.
source: As described above, unc-42 single mutants have mild defects in execution of cholinergic fate of these neurons (unc-17/VAChT expression) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The LIM homeobox gene lim-4 was previously shown to be expressed in a number of mostly cholinergic head sensory, inter-, and motor neurons and acts as a terminal selector to control AWB and SMB neuron identity.
source: The LIM homeobox gene lim-4 was previously shown to be expressed in a number of mostly cholinergic head sensory, inter-, and motor neurons and acts as a terminal selector to control AWB and SMB neuron identity (Sagasti et al., 1999; Kim et al., 2015; Alqadah et al., 2015; Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claim: lim-4 single mutants have mild defects in the execution of cholinergic fate in the RMF and RMH head motor neurons.
source: We find that like unc-42 single mutants lim-4 single mutants have mild defects in the execution of cholinergic fate in the RMF and RMH head motor neurons (unc-17/VAChT expression) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Defects in cholinergic fate in RMF and RMH are strongly enhanced in unc-42; lim-4 double mutant.
source: These defects are strongly enhanced in unc-42; lim-4 double mutant (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3 demonstrating genetic interaction.

claim: The hlh-34 gene, a bHLH-PAS transcription factor, is exclusively expressed in the AVH neuron throughout the life of the AVH neuron.
source: The hlh-34 gene, a bHLH-PAS transcription factor, is exclusively expressed in the AVH neuron throughout the life of the AVH neuron (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of hlh-34 expression.

claim: hlh-34 mutant animals show AVH differentiation defects that match those observed in unc-42 animals.
source: We used CRISPR/Cas9 to engineer a loss-of-function allele of hlh-34 (Figure 13A) and found AVH differentiation defects in these animals (Figure 13B, C) that match those observed in unc-42 animals.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 13.

claim: hlh-34; unc-42 double null mutants show strongly enhanced mutant phenotypes.
source: Moreover, hlh-34; unc-42 double null mutants show strongly enhanced mutant phenotypes (Figure 13C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 13C demonstrating genetic interaction.

claim: UNC-42 may cooperate with HLH-34 to specify AVH identity.
source: Hence, UNC-42 may cooperate with HLH-34 to specify AVH identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data.

claim: unc-62/Meis and ceh-20/Pbx are co-expressed with unc-42 exclusively in the AIB neurons.
source: In the glutamatergic AIB interneuron, we identified two potential collaborators for unc-42, the Meis-type homeobox gene unc-62 and the Pbx-type homeobox gene ceh-20, both of which co-expressed with unc-42 exclusively in the AIB neurons (Reilly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on expression pattern analysis with citation to Reilly et al., 2020.

claim: unc-62/Meis and ceh-20/Pbx mutant animals phenocopy the AIB differentiation defects observed in unc-42 mutant animals.
source: unc-62/Meis and ceh-20/Pbx mutant animals phenocopy the AIB differentiation defects observed in unc-42 mutant animals (Figure 13D–I).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 13.

claim: Loss-of-function alleles of unc-62 and ceh-20 result in defects in expression of several key identity features of AIB, including loss of glutamatergic identity (eat-4/VGLUT expression) and loss of expression of several innexin genes.
source: Specifically, loss-of-function alleles of both genes results in defects in expression of several key identity features of AIB, including loss of glutamatergic identity (eat-4/VGLUT expression) and loss of expression of several innexin genes (Figure 13D, E, G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 13.

claim: In the SIB lateral motor neurons, the differentiation defects observed in unc-42 mutants are phenocopied by loss of the ceh-24 homeobox gene.
source: Lastly, in the SIB lateral motor neurons, the differentiation defects observed in unc-42 mutants are phenocopied by loss of the ceh-24 homeobox gene (Schwarz and Bringmann, 2017), suggesting that these two transcription factors may cooperate in the SIB neurons.
evidence: This is based on citation to Schwarz and Bringmann, 2017.

claim: ceh-24 is expressed in SMB, not SMD.
source: However, using the cell identification and cell fate tool NeuroPAL, we found that ceh-24 is expressed in SMB, not SMD (Reilly et al., 2020), and, correspondingly, that in ceh-24 null mutants, SMB and not SMD differentiation is defective (Figure 13—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on NeuroPAL analysis shown in Figure 13—figure supplement 1.

claim: In ceh-24 null mutants, SMB and not SMD differentiation is defective.
source: However, using the cell identification and cell fate tool NeuroPAL, we found that ceh-24 is expressed in SMB, not SMD (Reilly et al., 2020), and, correspondingly, that in ceh-24 null mutants, SMB and not SMD differentiation is defective (Figure 13—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 13—figure supplement 1.

claim: The specificity of UNC-42 activity is determined by cell-type-specific collaboration of UNC-42 with distinct cofactors.
source: As summarized in Figure 14, we conclude that the specificity of UNC-42 activity is determined by cell-type-specific collaboration of UNC-42 with distinct cofactors.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of UNC-42 cofactors in different neuron types.

claim: The expression of ceh-24, cfi-1, and unc-3 reporter genes is strongly affected in unc-42 mutants.
source: We indeed find that the expression of ceh-24, cfi-1, and unc-3 reporter genes is strongly affected in unc-42 mutants (Figure 13—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 13—figure supplement 2.

claim: fax-1 has previously been shown to be regulated by unc-42.
source: Moreover, fax-1 has previously been shown to be regulated by unc-42 (Wightman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work.

claim: hlh-34, unc-62/Meis, and ceh-20/Pbx expression is unaffected in AVH and AIB, respectively, in unc-42 mutants.
source: In contrast, hlh-34, unc-62/Meis, and ceh-20/Pbx expression is unaffected in AVH and AIB, respectively.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of reporter expression.

claim: Several of the factors that collaborate with unc-42 in a neuron-type-specific manner are also expressed in synaptically connected neurons.
source: Intriguingly, several of the factors that collaborate with unc-42 in a neuron-type-specific manner are also expressed in synaptically connected neurons.
evidence: This is based on analysis of expression patterns and synaptic connectivity.

claim: The ceh-24 NK2-type homeobox gene cooperates with unc-42 in the SAA and SIB neurons.
source: This includes the ceh-24 NK2-type homeobox gene, which cooperates with unc-42 in the SAA and SIB neurons (summarized in Figure 14).
evidence: This is based on genetic interaction data.

claim: ceh-24 is also expressed in the RME, SIA, and SMB neurons.
source: In addition, ceh-24 is also expressed in the RME, SIA, and SMB neurons (Reilly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on citation to Reilly et al., 2020.

claim: All five ceh-24 expression neurons are interconnected more heavily than expected by chance.
source: All five ceh-24 expression neurons are interconnected more heavily than expected by chance. This correlation is observed using the analysis as done by Arnatkeviciute et al., as well as the NDGE analysis that we described above (Supplementary file 1, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of synaptic connectivity.

claim: The LIM homeobox gene lim-4 collaborates with unc-42 in some neurons, but is also expressed in additional sets of synaptically connected neurons.
source: Similarly, the LIM homeobox gene lim-4 collaborates with unc-42 in some neurons, but is also expressed in additional sets of synaptically connected neurons (Supplementary file 1, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on expression pattern analysis and synaptic connectivity analysis.

claim: The sites of expression of the COE-type transcription factor unc-3 are significantly enriched for synaptically connected neurons based on the approach by Arnatkeviciute et al. and NDGE analysis.
source: Lastly, the sites of expression of the COE-type transcription factor unc-3, an apparent cofactor for unc-42 in command interneurons (see above), are also significantly enriched for synaptically connected neurons based on the approach by Arnatkeviciute et al. and NDGE analysis.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of synaptic connectivity.

claim: The UNC-3(+) neurons include the UNC-42(+) command interneurons, but also UNC-42(-) ventral cord motor neurons that are directly innervated by command interneurons.
source: These UNC-3(+) neurons include the UNC-42(+) command interneurons, but also UNC-42(-) ventral cord motor neurons that are directly innervated by command interneurons.
evidence: This is based on expression pattern analysis and connectome data.

claim: The C. elegans connectome can be deconstructed into a series of overlapping groups of interconnected neurons whose interconnectivity is defined by 'circuit organizer transcription factors'.
source: Taken together, one can imagine that the C. elegans connectome can be deconstructed into a series of overlapping groups of interconnected neurons whose interconnectivity is defined by what we propose to call 'circuit organizer transcription factors' (Figure 14).
evidence: This is a conceptual model proposed based on the comprehensive analysis of transcription factor expression and synaptic connectivity.

claim: unc-42 appears to act as a terminal selector of neuronal identity in each neuron type it is expressed in.
source: First, from the perspective of individual unc-42(+) neurons, unc-42 appears to act as a terminal selector of neuronal identity in each neuron type it is expressed in.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of unc-42 function in controlling multiple aspects of neuronal identity.

claim: unc-42 is not required for neuron generation or adoption of panneuronal features.
source: unc-42 is not required for neuron generation or adoption of panneuronal features, but it initiates their respective terminal differentiation program, as inferred by the requirement of unc-42 for the expression of a host of terminal marker genes of the respective neuron classes.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing normal neuron generation and panneuronal marker expression in unc-42 mutants.

claim: Based on its continuous expression throughout larval and adult stages, UNC-42 likely also maintains the expression of its effector genes.
source: Based on its continuous expression throughout larval and adult stages, UNC-42 likely also maintains the expression of its effector genes, as demonstrated for other terminal selector-type transcription factors (Leyva-Díaz and Hobert, 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern and comparison to other terminal selectors.

claim: unc-42 mutants display locomotory defects that phenocopy defects observed upon surgical removal of individual unc-42(+) neurons.
source: Consequently, unc-42 mutants display locomotory defects that phenocopy defects observed upon surgical removal of individual unc-42(+) neurons.
evidence: This is based on behavioral analysis and comparison to ablation studies.

claim: Removal of individual unc-42-target genes phenocopies behavioral defects observed upon loss of unc-42.
source: Moreover, removal of individual unc-42-target genes phenocopies behavioral defects observed upon loss of unc-42, further corroborating the relevance of unc-42 and its targets in controlling neuron function.
evidence: This is based on behavioral analysis of target gene mutants.

claim: The identification of unc-42 as a terminal selector in many different neuron types corroborates the importance of homeobox genes in neuronal identity specification.
source: The identification of unc-42 as a terminal selector in many different neuron types also corroborates the importance of homeobox genes in neuronal identity specification, inferred from past studies of homeobox gene expression and function in C. elegans (Hobert, 2016; Reilly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the current study and citations to previous work.

claim: unc-42 interacts with different collaborating terminal selectors in different neuron types to specify the expression of distinct downstream target genes.
source: The second common theme of UNC-42 function lies in its ability to interact with different collaborating terminal selectors in different neuron types to specify the expression of distinct downstream target genes.
evidence: This is based on the comprehensive analysis of genetic interactions and binding site enrichment.

claim: In the unc-42 single mutant, both the penetrance and expressivity of effects on terminal marker of neuronal identity vary from target gene to target gene and from cell to cell.
source: The examination of unc-42 function in many different neuron types, as well as the genetic interactions with collaborating terminal selectors, adds a number of important nuances to the terminal selector concept: in the unc-42 single mutant, both the penetrance and expressivity of effects on terminal marker of neuronal identity vary from target gene to target gene and from cell to cell and even vary on the same target gene in different cells.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of marker expression defects throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mild effects in the unc-42 single mutants can be enhanced by removing a co-terminal selector in several cases.
source: In several cases, we have explicitly shown that mild effects in the unc-42 single mutants can be enhanced by removing a co-terminal selector.
evidence: This is based on genetic interaction data shown in Figures 3 and 13.

claim: The cell- and target gene-specific effects of a terminal selector are likely a reflection of the distinct mechanisms by which transcription factors activate their targets.
source: These cell- and target gene-specific effects of a terminal selector are likely a reflection of the distinct mechanisms by which transcription factors activate their targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the variable effects observed in unc-42 mutants.

claim: In cases where UNC-42 binds to its target with a cofactor in a strictly cooperative manner, removal of either UNC-42 or its cofactor(s) is expected to result in fully penetrant and expressive defects.
source: In those cases where UNC-42 binds to its target with a cofactor in a strictly cooperative manner, removal of either UNC-42 or its cofactor(s) is expected to result in fully penetrant and expressive defects.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on known examples of cooperative DNA binding.

claim: A precedent for cooperative binding is the TTX-3/CEH-10 heterodimer that cooperatively binds to cis-regulatory motifs present in AIY neuron-expressed genes.
source: A precedent for such scenario is the TTX-3/CEH-10 heterodimer that cooperative binds to cis-regulatory motifs present in AIY neuron-expressed genes (Wenick and Hobert, 2004).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work.

claim: UNC-42 may also interact with other target genes in the context of a 'transcription factor collective', in which transcription factors bind separately to their target promoter and the loss of individual components of the collective can be partially compensated for by other transcription factors in the collective.
source: In contrast, UNC-42 may also interact with other target genes in the context of a 'transcription factor collective' (Junion et al., 2012), in which transcription factors bind separately to their target promoter and the loss of individual components of the collective can be partially compensated for by other transcription factors in the collective.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the concept of transcription factor collectives.

claim: One example for the transcription factor collective model of terminal selector function in C. elegans neurons is observed in dopaminergic neurons.
source: One example for this model of terminal selector function in C. elegans neurons is observed in dopaminergic neurons (Doitsidou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work.

claim: UNC-42 acts in the manner of a transcription factor collective in the majority of neuronal cell types.
source: Based on the phenotypic analysis described here, we envision that UNC-42 acts in this manner in the majority of neuronal cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the variable penetrance and expressivity of defects in unc-42 mutants.

claim: unc-42 may facilitate intra-strata connectivity, thereby ensuring the coordination of information flow through distinct neighborhoods of the nerve ring.
source: Interestingly, the processes of unc-42(+) neurons traverse distinct neighborhoods ('strata') of the nerve ring (Moyle et al., 2021; Brittin et al., 2021), indicating that unc-42 may facilitate intra-strata connectivity, thereby ensuring the coordination of information flow through distinct neighborhoods.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unc-42(+) neurons are in different strata but are synaptically connected.

claim: unc-42 coordinates both circuit assembly and signaling within the unc-42(+) circuit.
source: Taken together with the effect of unc-42 on neurotransmitter, neurotransmitter receptor, and neuropeptide expression, unc-42 therefore coordinates both circuit assembly and signaling within this circuit.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of unc-42 function.

claim: A detailed comparison of expression patterns of transcription factors and synaptic connectivity reveals several transcription factors whose expression is enriched in synaptically connected neurons.
source: A detailed comparison of expression patterns of transcription factors and synaptic connectivity reveals several transcription factors whose expression is, like unc-42, enriched in synaptically connected neurons.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of transcription factor expression and synaptic connectivity.

claim: Many transcription factors enriched in synaptically connected neurons have been shown to be required to control the identity of individual neurons that express these transcription factors.
source: Many of these transcription factors have been shown to be required to control the identity of individual neurons that express these transcription factors, that is, they act as terminal selectors that coordinate the expression of many/most/all terminal identity features of a neuron.
evidence: This is based on previous literature on terminal selector function.

claim: The unc-3 terminal selector is expressed in and functions to specify synaptically connected neurons, namely head and tail command interneurons and ventral nerve cord motor neurons.
source: For example, we had previously already noted that the unc-3 terminal selector is expressed in and functions to specify synaptically connected neurons, namely head and tail command interneurons and ventral nerve cord motor neurons, which are innervated by these head and tail commend neurons (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work.

claim: unc-3 and unc-42 expression and function overlap in head command interneurons.
source: unc-3 and unc-42 expression and function overlap in head command interneurons.
evidence: This is based on expression pattern analysis and genetic interaction data.

claim: A synaptic pathway from sensory input by the polymodal ASH neuron to motor neuron innervation of body wall muscle can be defined by the integration of two sets of synaptically interconnected neurons that are specified by unc-3 and unc-42.
source: Hence, a synaptic pathway from sensory input by the polymodal ASH neuron to motor neuron innervation of body wall muscle can be defined by the integration of two sets of synaptically interconnected neurons that are specified by two transcription factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlapping expression and function of unc-3 and unc-42.

claim: Synaptic pathways from sensory to various head motor neurons, and hence, head muscle are defined by overlapping sets of unc-42(+) and ceh-24(+) neurons.
source: Similarly, synaptic pathways from sensory to various head motor neurons, and hence, head muscle are defined by overlapping sets of unc-42(+) and ceh-24(+) neurons (Figure 14B).
evidence: This is inferred from the overlapping expression patterns and synaptic connectivity shown in Figure 14B.

claim: The association of transcription factors with synaptic connectivity appears to be evident in other nervous systems as well, from other invertebrates to the vertebrate central nervous system.
source: The association of transcription factors with synaptic connectivity appears to be evident in other nervous systems as well, from other invertebrates to the vertebrate central nervous system.
evidence: This is based on citations to examples from other organisms.

claim: Motor neuron innervation and their target tissue have been found to rely on matching HOX cluster gene expression.
source: In the perhaps simplest example, motor neuron innervation and their target tissue have been found to rely on matching HOX cluster gene expression (Arenkiel et al., 2004; Hessinger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claim: Matching Hoxc8 gene expression specifies motor-sensory neuron connectivity in proprioceptive circuits of the mouse spinal cord.
source: Similarly, matching Hoxc8 gene expression specifies motor-sensory neuron connectivity in proprioceptive circuits of the mouse spinal cord (Shin et al., 2020) and Shox2 gene specifies interconnected neuron types in the spinal cord (Ha and Dougherty, 2018).
evidence: This is based on citation to Shin et al., 2020.

claim: Shox2 gene specifies interconnected neuron types in the spinal cord.
source: Similarly, matching Hoxc8 gene expression specifies motor-sensory neuron connectivity in proprioceptive circuits of the mouse spinal cord (Shin et al., 2020) and Shox2 gene specifies interconnected neuron types in the spinal cord (Ha and Dougherty, 2018).

claim: The Otx2 homeobox gene was found to define and specify neurons in a subcircuit of the habenulo-interpeduncular system.
source: In the central brain, the Otx2 homeobox gene was found to define and specify neurons in a subcircuit of the habenulo-interpeduncular system (Ruiz-Reig et al., 2019) and the homeobox Dbx1 specifies functionally interconnected neurons in the hypothalamus (Sokolowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citation to Ruiz-Reig et al., 2019.

claim: The homeobox Dbx1 specifies functionally interconnected neurons in the hypothalamus.
source: In the central brain, the Otx2 homeobox gene was found to define and specify neurons in a subcircuit of the habenulo-interpeduncular system (Ruiz-Reig et al., 2019) and the homeobox Dbx1 specifies functionally interconnected neurons in the hypothalamus (Sokolowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citation to Sokolowski et al., 2015.

claim: The Phox2 gene controls the differentiation of a class of interconnected neurons that form a sensory reflex circuit in the autonomous nervous system.
source: Perhaps the most striking example is the Phox2 gene, which controls the differentiation of a class of interconnected neurons that form a sensory reflex circuit in the autonomous nervous system (Dauger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on citation to Dauger et al., 2003.

claim: In the nervous system of Drosophila males, the transcription factor Fruitless is thought to assemble neurons into functional circuitry.
source: Another very specialized example can be found in the nervous system of Drosophila males, where the transcription factor Fruitless is thought to assemble neurons into functional circuitry (Stockinger et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on citation to Stockinger et al., 2005.

claim: With the exception of Fruitless, all the transcription factors associated with circuit connectivity in other organisms are homeobox genes.
source: It is remarkable that, with the exception of Fruitless, all the above-mentioned factors are homeobox genes, like unc-42, which is in line with their striking predominance in neuronal identity control (Reilly et al., 2020).
